drills.los_text: compare factor-based strategies to market-capitalization-weighted indexing

questions.stem: Market-capitalization-weighted indexing is most likely based on:

options.A: An arbitrary weighting scheme.
options.B: A single-factor model, the CAPM.
options.C: No theoretical foundation.

rationales.A: Capitalization weighting is not arbitrary: each security's weight is its share of total market value, which is the market portfolio of the capital asset pricing model. Investors in such strategies seek market return, otherwise known as beta exposure, and do not seek outperformance, known as alpha.
rationales.B: Investors in index-based strategies may seek market return, otherwise known as beta exposure, and do not seek outperformance, known as alpha. A focus on beta is based on a single-factor model: the capital asset pricing model (CAPM). Index-based strategies based on more than a single factor, and on a single factor other than beta, are becoming more popular as investors gain an understanding of what drives investment returns.
rationales.C: There is a theoretical foundation. Capitalization weighting delivers beta exposure, and a focus on beta rests on a single-factor model, the capital asset pricing model, in which the market portfolio is held in proportion to market value.

questions.stem: The Fama and French (2015) model of US equity market returns is most likely based on:

options.A: the market factor alone, refining the CAPM beta estimate.
options.B: market, size, value, momentum, and low volatility.
options.C: market, size, value, operating profitability, and investment intensity.

rationales.A: The 2015 model is a five-factor extension of the CAPM, not a single-factor refinement of it. The market risk premium from the CAPM is only the first of its five factors.
rationales.B: Momentum and low volatility are not among the five factors in this model. Operating profitability and investment intensity, measured as total asset growth, complete the set alongside the market risk premium from the CAPM, size, and the book-to-market ratio.
rationales.C: The five factors discussed in Fama and French (2015) that explain US equity market returns are the market risk premium from the CAPM, size, the book-to-market ratio (value or growth style classification), operating profitability, and investment intensity measured as total asset growth. Index-based strategies based on more than a single factor, and on a single factor other than beta, are becoming more popular as investors gain an understanding of what drives investment returns.

questions.stem: 'Smart beta' strategies most likely refer to:

options.A: pure alpha generation, uncorrelated with systematic factors.
options.B: leverage applied to a capitalization-weighted index.
options.C: factor investing, with exposure to value, size, momentum, volatility, and quality.

rationales.A: Smart beta is systematic factor exposure, to such factors as value, size, momentum, volatility, and quality, which is the opposite of a return uncorrelated with any factor. These strategies provide an expected return based on exposure to those factors rather than factor-free alpha.
rationales.B: Leverage on a capitalization-weighted index amplifies market beta but leaves the factor exposure unchanged. Smart beta instead means alternative, factor-based construction that still maintains the low-cost advantage of index funds.
rationales.C: Smart beta is a marketing label for factor investing. Although the concepts underlying factor investing have been known for a long time, investors' use of the technique increased dramatically over time, and there are many indexes and index-based investment vehicles that allow access to such factors as value, size, momentum, volatility, and quality. These strategies maintain the low-cost advantage of index funds but provide an expected return based on exposure to various factors.

questions.stem: A manager building a growth tilt in an index-based equity portfolio is most likely to select companies with:

options.A: High dividend yields.
options.B: Above-average net income growth and high P/Es.
options.C: Cyclical downturns in earnings.

rationales.A: High dividend yields are a value characteristic rather than a growth one. Value stocks are typically mature companies that pay cash out, so they combine low price-to-book and low price-to-earnings ratios with high dividend yields. Growth companies retain earnings to fund expansion and so pay little or nothing out.
rationales.B: Growth stocks are generally associated with companies that have an above-average net income growth rate and high price-to-earnings ratios. The high multiple is the market capitalizing earnings expected to arrive in the future rather than earnings already reported.
rationales.C: A cyclical downturn points to value, not growth. Value stocks are generally associated with mature companies that have stable net income or are experiencing a cyclical downturn, and that depressed earnings picture is part of why they trade at low price-to-book and low price-to-earnings ratios with high dividend yields.

questions.stem: A manager building a value tilt in an index-based equity portfolio is most likely to select:

options.A: Mature companies with stable or cyclically depressed net income.
options.B: Companies with high earnings growth rates.
options.C: Companies with high P/Es.

rationales.A: Value stocks are generally associated with mature companies that have stable net income or are experiencing a cyclical downturn. They frequently show low price-to-book and low price-to-earnings ratios as well as high dividend yields, because the price paid reflects earnings already in hand rather than earnings expected to grow.
rationales.B: High growth rates describe growth stocks, which are associated with an above-average net income growth rate and high price-to-earnings ratios. Value names sit at the opposite end of the same factor: mature, with stable net income, or cyclically depressed.
rationales.C: High price-to-earnings ratios are a growth characteristic. Low price-to-earnings ratios are typical of value stocks, alongside low price-to-book ratios and high dividend yields.

questions.stem: The Size factor tilt toward smaller size most likely involves:

options.A: Buying the largest-cap stocks.
options.B: Buying stocks with low float-adjusted market capitalization.
options.C: Buying stocks with low prices per share.

rationales.A: Buying the largest-cap names is a tilt in the opposite direction. A tilt toward smaller size involves buying stocks with low float-adjusted market capitalization, so the largest-cap stocks are exactly what such a tilt underweights.
rationales.B: A tilt toward smaller size involves buying stocks with low float-adjusted market capitalization. Float adjustment counts only the shares actually available to public investors, so closely held, government-held or otherwise restricted stock is excluded from the measure used to rank companies by size.
rationales.C: The Size factor is defined by low float-adjusted market capitalization, not by a low price per share. Price per share depends on how many shares a company has issued: a large company that has never split its stock can trade at a high price per share, and a large company with a very large share count can trade at a low one, so screening on price alone does not produce a small-size tilt.

questions.stem: The Momentum factor most likely attempts to capture:

options.A: Returns from stocks that recently lagged the market.
options.B: Further returns from stocks that recently outperformed.
options.C: Returns from prices reverting to prior levels.

rationales.A: Buying stocks that have recently underperformed the market is a contrarian or reversal strategy. Momentum does the opposite: it buys the stocks with above-average price increases in the prior period, on the expectation that recent relative strength continues.
rationales.B: Momentum attempts to capture further returns from stocks that have experienced an above-average increase in price during the prior period. It is generally defined by the amount of a stock's excess price return relative to the market over a specified time period, and it can be determined in various ways. In MSCI's Momentum Index family, for example, a stock's most recent 12-month and 6-month price performance are determined and then used to weight the securities in the index.
rationales.C: Reversion is the opposite of momentum. A reversion strategy expects recent price moves to unwind, whereas momentum seeks a continuation of returns from recent winners.

questions.stem: A screen for the Quality factor is most likely to include:

options.A: Firms with no profits.
options.B: Firms with high leverage.
options.C: Firms with consistent earnings growth and low debt to equity.

rationales.A: Unprofitable firms are what a Quality screen excludes. Quality stocks might include those with consistent earnings and dividend growth, high cash flow to earnings, and low debt-to-equity ratios, all of which presuppose profits that are being earned and grown.
rationales.B: High leverage is the opposite of what Quality looks for: low debt-to-equity ratios are one of the defining characteristics, alongside consistent earnings and dividend growth and high cash flow to earnings.
rationales.C: Quality stocks might include those with consistent earnings and dividend growth, high cash flow to earnings, and low debt-to-equity ratios. The cash-flow-to-earnings screen guards against reported earnings that are not backed by cash, and the low leverage screen against earnings that rest on a fragile balance sheet.

questions.stem: Within a classification of equity factor strategies, low volatility strategies are most likely:

options.A: Growth-oriented.
options.B: Return-oriented.
options.C: Risk-oriented.

rationales.A: Low volatility strategies are risk-focused, not growth-focused. Growth is a return-oriented factor aimed at capturing a return premium, while a low volatility tilt is aimed at lowering downside risk.
rationales.B: Low volatility belongs to the risk-oriented family, not the return-oriented one. Return-oriented factor strategies seek to capture a return premium; risk-oriented strategies such as low volatility seek to reduce downside volatility and overall portfolio risk.
rationales.C: Low volatility is risk-oriented: investors seek to lower their downside risk. Volatility is often measured as the standard deviation of stock returns. Risk-oriented strategies take several forms aimed at reducing downside volatility and overall portfolio risk — volatility weighting, for instance, holds all of an index's constituents and then weights them by the inverse of their relative price volatility, so the least volatile names carry the most weight.

questions.stem: Factor tilts applied by investors to their portfolios are most likely to:

options.A: Overweight and underweight risk factors based on market judgment.
options.B: Require continuous daily rebalancing to exact factor weights.
options.C: Guarantee outperformance when the tilted factor carries a premium.

rationales.A: Many investors apply factor tilts — intentionally overweighting and underweighting certain risk factors — to their portfolios based on their judgment of market conditions. Index-based factor strategies can be used in place of, or to complement, a more traditional market-cap-weighted indexed portfolio.
rationales.B: Factor tilts are judgment-based overweights and underweights of risk factors; they do not require continuous daily rebalancing to exact factor weights. An index-based factor strategy is rebalanced on the index's own published schedule, and the active element sits in the choice of factor and the size of the tilt rather than in daily maintenance.
rationales.C: A factor premium is not guaranteed over any given horizon: even strong risk factors experience periods of underperformance. A tilt reflects the investor's judgment of market conditions, not assured outperformance, and it is precisely those observed periods of underperformance that have led many investors toward multi-factor approaches.

questions.stem: Relative to broad market-cap weighting, index-based factor strategies are most likely to:

options.A: Concentrate risk exposures.
options.B: Diversify risk identically.
options.C: Spread risk more broadly.

rationales.A: Relative to broad-market-cap weighting, factor-based strategies tend to concentrate risk exposures, leaving investors exposed during periods when a chosen risk factor is out of favor. The observation that even strong risk factors experience periods of underperformance has led many investors toward multi-factor approaches.
rationales.B: A factor strategy does not diversify in the same way as the broad cap-weighted market. By construction it holds more of the stocks that score well on the chosen factor and less of, or none of, the rest, so its risk exposures are concentrated rather than identical to the market's.
rationales.C: Concentration is the trade-off a factor tilt accepts, not something it avoids. Spreading risk more broadly than a single-factor tilt does is what a multi-factor approach attempts to recover, and the need for it follows from the concentration the single tilt introduced.

questions.stem: The weighting of each company in a fundamental factor index is most likely based on:

options.A: Equal weights for every constituent.
options.B: Each company's current market price.
options.C: A cluster of company fundamentals such as book value, cash flow, and sales.

rationales.A: Equal weighting is a different weighting scheme. Fundamental indexing weights each company on a cluster of company fundamentals — book value, cash flow, revenue, sales, dividends and employee count — so it depends heavily on company characteristics rather than removing any dependence on them.
rationales.B: Weighting by current market price is exactly what fundamental indexing rejects, because that is what a cap-weighted index already does. Fundamental indexing weights by measures drawn from the financial statements instead, which is what breaks the link between a company's weight and the market's current valuation of it.
rationales.C: Arnott, Hsu, and Moore (2005) proposed using a cluster of company fundamentals — book value, cash flow, revenue, sales, dividends and employee count — as the basis for weighting each company. A separate weighting is developed for each fundamental measure, and for each company the weightings are then averaged across all of the measures. Over a 43-year period a fundamental index would have outperformed a related cap-weighted index by an average of almost 200 basis points per year; the authors add that this should not necessarily be considered alpha, because the fundamental portfolio provides heightened exposure to the Value and Size factors.

questions.stem: Even though factor strategies are labeled 'passive', they most likely involve:

options.A: Continuous active decisions, as in discretionary stock picking.
options.B: Active decisions on factor exposure made up front.
options.C: No active decision making at any stage.

rationales.A: The active decision making concentrates at the design stage rather than running continuously. Factor selection, weighting and rebalancing are set out in rules and then applied, so ongoing management is not the continuous discretionary security selection of conventional active management.
rationales.B: Index-based factor strategies may be labeled passive, but they frequently involve active decision making: decisions on the timing and degree of factor exposure are being made. As Jacobs and Levy (2014) note, the difference between index-based factor investing and conventional active management is that with the former, active management takes place up front rather than continuously. Factor selection, weighting and rebalancing tend to be transparent, but decisions are still being made, and the possible risks include ease of replication by other investors, which can produce overcrowding.
rationales.C: Choosing which factors to tilt toward, how much exposure to take and when to take it involves genuine active decisions. What makes the passive label defensible is only that those decisions are made up front and then applied by rule, not that no decisions are made.

drills.los_text: compare different approaches to index-based equity strategies

questions.stem: Index-based strategies are most likely:

options.A: rule-based and transparent.
options.B: costliest because of frequent reconstitution trading.
options.C: reliant on discretionary security selection.

rationales.A: Index-based strategies are rule-based, transparent strategies that do not involve identifying mispriced individual securities but instead seek to replicate the performance of an index. The indexes replicated include broad market indexes, such as the S&P 500 Index, the Nikkei 225, and the FTSE 100, as well as indexes tailored more to a factor exposure, such as the Russell 1000 Growth and Russell 1000 Value Indexes. The main advantages of index-based investing are low costs, diversification, and tax efficiency.
rationales.B: Low cost is a defining feature of index-based investing, not a weakness of it, and it sits alongside diversification and tax efficiency as one of the approach's three main advantages. Index reconstitution does generate some trading, but that trading is modest relative to the turnover of a discretionary active strategy, so index-based strategies sit at the low-cost end of the spectrum rather than the high-cost end.
rationales.C: Discretionary identification of mispriced individual securities is precisely what an index-based strategy does not do; that is the work of active management. Index-based strategies are instead rule-based and transparent, seeking to replicate the performance of a chosen index rather than to beat it through security selection, and it is that rule-based construction that delivers their low costs, diversification, and tax efficiency.

questions.stem: Pooled investment vehicles for index exposure most likely include:

options.A: the single largest stock in the index.
options.B: open-end mutual funds and exchange-traded funds.
options.C: no pooled vehicle, only direct replication.

rationales.A: A single stock cannot deliver index exposure, however large its weight in the index, because the return of one company is not the return of the basket. A pooled vehicle works precisely because the fund holds the diversified basket of index constituents on the investor's behalf, which is also what produces the diversification advantage of index-based investing.
rationales.B: Pooled investment vehicles for index exposure are conventional open-end mutual funds and exchange-traded funds (ETFs). The Qualidex Fund, started in 1970, was the first open-end index mutual fund available to retail investors and was designed to track the Dow Jones Industrial Average. The Vanguard S&P 500 Index Fund, started in 1975, was the first retail index fund to attract investors on a large scale. ETFs are the other form of pooled investment vehicle: the first ETF was launched in the Canadian market in 1990 to track the return of 35 large stocks listed on the Toronto Stock Exchange, and ETFs were introduced in the US market in 1993.
rationales.C: Pooled index vehicles have existed for decades. Open-end index mutual funds date from the Qualidex Fund in 1970, which tracked the Dow Jones Industrial Average, and the Vanguard S&P 500 Index Fund of 1975 was the first to attract retail investors on a large scale. ETFs followed, launching in Canada in 1990 and in the United States in 1993. Direct replication of an index is possible but it is not the only route, and for most investors the pooled routes are cheaper and simpler.

questions.stem: The advantages of the ETF structure over a conventional mutual fund are most likely:

options.A: no real advantage, only marketing novelty.
options.B: intraday trading, low fees, and tax efficiency.
options.C: no cost advantage, since ETFs are always dearer.

rationales.A: The advantages of the ETF structure are structural rather than cosmetic: ease of trading throughout the day like a stock, low management fees, tax efficiency, the ability to buy on margin, the ability to take short positions, and flexibility in tracking a wide array of indexes. Margin borrowing and short positions in particular are not available with traditional open-end mutual funds at all, so they are genuine capability differences rather than presentation.
rationales.B: Advantages of the ETF structure include ease of trading throughout the day like a stock, low management fees, and tax efficiency. Unlike with traditional open-end mutual funds, ETF shares can be bought using margin borrowing, and investors can take short positions in an ETF. ETFs also offer flexibility in that they track a wide array of indexes. All else equal, in jurisdictions that require capital gains and losses to be passed through to investors, such as the United States, an ETF has greater tax efficiency than a similarly managed mutual fund: a mutual fund manager must sell portfolio holdings to fulfill shareholder redemptions, creating a taxable event in which gains and losses are realized, whereas an ETF can accommodate those redemptions through an in-kind delivery of stock.
rationales.C: ETF expense ratios are typically competitive with, and for long-term holders slightly lower than, those of otherwise equivalent conventional open-end index mutual funds, so the ownership-cost comparison favors the ETF rather than penalizing it. The one qualification runs the other way and is a trading cost rather than an ownership cost: brokerage fees associated with frequent investor trades into ETF shares can negate the expense ratio advantage.

questions.stem: The disadvantages of the ETF structure are most likely:

options.A: bid-offer spreads, commissions, and illiquidity risk.
options.B: none, as the structure has no drawbacks.
options.C: no liquidity risk, which the sponsor guarantees.

rationales.A: Disadvantages of the ETF structure include the need to buy at the offer and sell at the bid price, commission costs, and the risk of an illiquid market when the investor needs to buy or sell the actual ETF shares. The decision whether to use a conventional open-end mutual fund or an ETF often comes down to cost and flexibility: an investor seeking to mimic an index must identify a suitable tracking security, and long-term investors benefit from the slightly lower expense ratios of ETFs relative to otherwise equivalent conventional open-end mutual funds. The brokerage fees associated with frequent investor trades into ETF shares, however, can negate that expense ratio advantage.
rationales.B: The ETF structure carries real costs that a conventional open-end mutual fund does not. Shares are bought at the offer and sold at the bid, so the spread is paid on each round trip; commissions are charged on each trade, and frequent trading can negate the ETF's expense ratio advantage; and the secondary market in the shares can be illiquid at the moment the investor needs to transact.
rationales.C: No sponsor guarantees a liquid market in ETF shares at all times. The risk of an illiquid market when the investor needs to buy or sell the actual ETF shares is one of the structure's acknowledged disadvantages, alongside paying the bid-offer spread and commission costs, and secondary-market liquidity can thin precisely when investors most need to trade. The authorized participant's creation and redemption mechanism links the share price to the value of the underlying basket but is not a promise of liquidity on demand.

questions.stem: The role of the authorized participant in an ETF structure is best described as:

options.A: a retail investor buying shares from the fund at NAV.
options.B: a market maker and creation-redemption intermediary.
options.C: a role that does not exist, as the manager deals directly.

rationales.A: Retail investors buy and sell ETF shares in the secondary market at market prices, not from the fund at net asset value. The authorized participant is an institutional intermediary, and it transacts with the fund manager in kind, delivering or receiving a basket of the underlying stocks rather than cash at NAV.
rationales.B: An ETF has a unique structure that requires a fund manager as well as an authorized participant who can deliver the assets to the manager. The role of the authorized participant is to be the market maker for the ETF and the intermediary between investors and the ETF fund manager when shares are created or redeemed. To create shares of the ETF, the authorized participant delivers a basket of the underlying stocks to the fund manager and in exchange receives shares of the ETF that can be sold to the public. When shares need to be redeemed, the process is reversed: the authorized participant delivers shares of the ETF in exchange for a basket of the underlying stocks that can then be sold in the market. That in-kind mechanism is what gives the ETF its tax efficiency relative to a mutual fund, which must sell holdings and realize gains to meet redemptions.
rationales.C: The ETF structure is defined by the presence of this intermediary: the fund manager does not transact with each investor. The authorized participant stands between investors and the fund manager, making a market in the shares and handling creations and redemptions in kind, while ordinary investors trade with one another in the secondary market.

questions.stem: Factor-based ETFs' share of the approximately $7 trillion of global equity ETF assets under management as of the fourth quarter of 2022 is closest to:

rationales.A: Approximately 3% was the share held by actively managed ETFs as of the fourth quarter of 2022, with another 3% in other approaches. Factor-based ETFs were a far larger segment at 17% of the roughly $7 trillion in global equity ETF assets under management.
rationales.B: Factor-based ETFs have become a large segment of the market, accounting for 17% of the approximately $7 trillion in global equity ETF assets under management as of the fourth quarter of 2022. The remainder of that market was conventional index-tracking ETFs at 77%, actively managed ETFs at 3%, and other approaches at 3%. Factor-based ETFs provide exposure to such single factors as Size, Value, Momentum, Quality, Volatility, and Yield, and multifactor products exist as well, such as an ETF emphasizing combined exposure to the Size, Value, Momentum, Quality, and Volatility factors.
rationales.C: Approximately 77% was the share held by conventional index-tracking ETFs as of the fourth quarter of 2022, which remains the dominant segment. Factor-based ETFs accounted for 17% of the approximately $7 trillion market, with actively managed ETFs and other approaches at roughly 3% each.

questions.stem: As of December 2022, equity ETF assets under management as a percentage of the total value of securities outstanding is most likely:

options.A: highest in the US, at 12.5%.
options.B: over 50% in each region.
options.C: near 10% in every region.

rationales.A: Equity ETF assets under management as a percentage of the total value of securities outstanding in December 2022 was 12.5% in the United States, 7.1% in Europe, and 3.8% in Asia, so the United States led and the other regions trailed well behind. Market share for fixed-income ETFs is much lower again. These figures reflect index ETFs as well as factor-based and other approaches, and taken together ETFs represented just 9% of equity assets across the United States, Europe, and Asia Pacific at the end of 2022.
rationales.B: Penetration is nowhere near half the market. The highest regional figure in December 2022 was the United States at 12.5%, followed by Europe at 7.1% and Asia at 3.8%, all comfortably under 15%, and ETFs represented just 9% of equity assets across the United States, Europe, and Asia Pacific combined at the end of 2022. Fixed-income ETF market share is lower still.
rationales.C: The shares are not similar across regions. The United States led at 12.5% in December 2022, roughly three and a half times Asia's 3.8% and well above Europe's 7.1%. The combined figure across the three regions was 9% of equity assets, which masks that spread rather than describing each region.

questions.stem: Open-end mutual fund regulation is most likely governed by:

options.A: the Investment Company Act in Europe and UCITS in the United States.
options.B: the same framework in every jurisdiction.
options.C: the Investment Company Act in the United States and UCITS in Europe.

rationales.A: The two frameworks are reversed here. The Investment Company Act of 1940 governs mutual funds in the United States, while Undertakings for Collective Investment in Transferable Securities (UCITS) is the European agreement, among countries of the European Union, that governs the management and sale of collective investment funds across European borders.
rationales.B: Mutual fund regulation is regional, not global. In the United States, mutual funds are governed by provisions of the Investment Company Act of 1940. In Europe, Undertakings for Collective Investment in Transferable Securities (UCITS) is an agreement among countries in the European Union that governs the management and sale of collective investment funds across European borders. The two regimes are separate instruments with different scope, so no single worldwide framework applies.
rationales.C: In the United States, mutual funds are governed by provisions of the Investment Company Act of 1940. In Europe, Undertakings for Collective Investment in Transferable Securities (UCITS) is an agreement among countries in the European Union that governs the management and sale of collective investment funds, that is, mutual funds, across European borders. The UCITS framework is what allows a fund authorized in one member state to be marketed throughout the Union.

questions.stem: The needs analysis for selecting an index-based mutual fund most likely involves:

options.A: the same steps as active fund selection.
options.B: a search for the lowest expense ratio first.
options.C: no analysis, as index funds are interchangeable.

rationales.A: Investors who want to invest in an index-based mutual fund must take the same steps as those investing in actively managed ones. First, a needs analysis must be undertaken to decide on the investor's return and risk objectives as well as investment constraints, and then to find a corresponding strategy. For example, risk-averse equity investors may seek a low volatility strategy, while investors looking to match the broad market may prefer an all-cap market-cap-weighted strategy. Once the need has been identified, it is likely that a mutual fund can be found or built to match that need.
rationales.B: Cost matters, but it is not the starting point. The needs analysis comes first: the investor's return and risk objectives and investment constraints are established, and only then is a corresponding strategy identified, after which expense ratios can be compared among the funds that actually match the need. Screening on cost first can deliver the cheapest fund tracking the wrong index, which is a worse outcome than paying a few basis points more for the right exposure.
rationales.C: Index funds are not interchangeable: they track different indexes, from broad market indexes to factor-tilted ones, and they differ in tracking quality, costs, and vehicle structure. That is why the selection process mirrors active fund selection, beginning with a needs analysis of return and risk objectives and constraints. A risk-averse investor may need a low volatility strategy while an investor seeking the broad market may need an all-cap market-cap-weighted one, and those are not substitutes.

questions.stem: A fund marketplace is best described as:

options.A: a service identical to that of a financial adviser.
options.B: a provider of personalized portfolio advice.
options.C: a brokerage offering funds from many providers.

rationales.A: The two are distinct value propositions. A fund marketplace is a brokerage company that offers funds from different providers, and its advantage is the ease of purchasing funds from several providers while maintaining a single account for streamlined record keeping. A financial adviser offers something a marketplace does not: the guidance needed to identify the strategy, together with a single account to house the fund shares and access to lower-cost share classes that may not be available to all investors.
rationales.B: Advice is what a financial adviser provides, not what defines a marketplace. The marketplace's value lies in breadth of selection, funds from many different providers, and in consolidated record keeping within a single account. An adviser, by contrast, provides the guidance needed to identify the strategy, houses the shares in a single account, and can gain access to lower-cost share classes that may not be available to all investors.
rationales.C: A fund marketplace is a brokerage company that offers funds from different providers. The advantage of buying a mutual fund from a fund marketplace is the ease of purchasing funds from different providers while maintaining a single account for streamlined record keeping. A financial adviser can also help in purchasing a fund, by offering the guidance needed to identify the strategy, providing the single account to house the fund shares, and gaining access to lower-cost share classes that may not be available to all investors.

questions.stem: Mutual fund manager responsibilities for index-based funds most likely include:

options.A: trading, cash management, corporate actions, proxy voting, and performance reporting.
options.B: computing and reporting fund performance only.
options.C: record keeping only, because index membership does not change.

rationales.A: Index-based strategies require constant maintenance and care: cash from dividends and investor flows must be reinvested, and the buys and sells required to match the additions and deletions of securities to the index must be executed. The portfolio manager of an index-based mutual fund therefore has most of the same responsibilities as a direct investor, including trading securities, managing cash, deciding how to proceed with corporate actions, voting proxies, and reporting performance. On top of that sit the rebalancing, reconstitution, and other changes needed to keep the portfolio in line with the index. Index-based mutual funds also bear costs in such areas as registration, custody, and audit, which are similar to those borne by actively managed mutual funds.
rationales.B: Computing and reporting the fund's performance is one duty among several, not the whole of the role. The same manager also trades securities, manages cash and dividend reinvestment, decides how to proceed with corporate actions, and votes proxies, and handles the rebalancing and reconstitution that keep the portfolio aligned with the index.
rationales.C: Index membership does change. Reconstitutions, rebalancings, investor flows, dividend reinvestment, and corporate actions all generate trades the manager must execute to keep the portfolio in line with the index, so trading securities is a core responsibility rather than an absent one. Record keeping is a benefit the fund structure provides to the investor, not the limit of the manager's duties.

questions.stem: Primary benefits of index-based mutual funds most likely are:

options.A: intraday tradability on an exchange.
options.B: performance fees aligned with index outperformance.
options.C: low costs and the convenience of the fund structure.

rationales.A: Intraday tradability on an exchange is the exchange-traded fund's distinguishing feature, not the mutual fund's; mutual fund shares transact at the end-of-day net asset value. Whatever route is used to buy mutual fund shares, the benefits of the index-based mutual fund are its low cost and the manager's handling of rebalancing, reconstitution, and other index-driven changes.
rationales.B: Index-based mutual funds charge low flat fees and do not pursue outperformance of the index, so there is no outperformance for a performance fee to be levied against. What draws investors is the combination of low cost and the convenience of the fund structure, including ease of investing and record keeping.
rationales.C: No matter how mutual fund shares are purchased, the primary benefits of index-based mutual funds are low costs and the convenience of the fund structure. The investment manager handles all the needed rebalancing, reconstitution, and other changes required to keep the investment portfolio in line with the index. The primary advantage provided by a mutual fund purchase is its ease of investing and record keeping, which the investor would otherwise have to arrange directly.

drills.los_text: compare different approaches to index-based equity investing

questions.stem: Derivatives-based approaches to index-based investing most likely offer:

options.A: no advantages over holding the underlying securities.
options.B: cost savings but no ability to provide leverage.
options.C: low cost, easy implementation, and leverage, with counterparty risk on uncleared contracts.

rationales.A: Low cost, easy implementation, and leverage are genuine advantages of derivatives-based index exposure. Beyond purchasing a third-party-sponsored pooled investment or building the portfolio themselves, investors can access index performance through derivatives such as options, swaps, or futures contracts. What derivatives bring is not an absence of advantages but an additional set of risks, including counterparty default risk for derivatives that are not traded on exchanges or cleared through a clearing house, and relative difficulty of access for individual investors.
rationales.B: Leverage is one of the principal advantages of derivatives, not something they lack. It arises through notional value amounts, which can be many times greater than the initial cash outlay. The genuine offsetting drawbacks are counterparty default risk on derivatives that are not exchange traded or cleared through a clearing house, the finite life of the contracts, and the difficulty individual investors can have in accessing them.
rationales.C: Derivative strategies are advantageous in that they can be low cost, easy to implement, and provide leverage. They also present a new set of risks, however, including counterparty default risk for derivatives that are not traded on exchanges or cleared through a clearing house, since in that case the investor's exposure runs to a single counterparty. Derivatives can also be relatively difficult for individual investors to access.

questions.stem: Relative to equity swaps on an index, exchange-traded index options and futures most likely differ in:

options.A: clearing arrangements, and hence counterparty default risk.
options.B: no material respect, counterparty risk profiles being identical.
options.C: name only, the instruments being structurally identical.

rationales.A: Options, swaps, and futures contracts can be found on many of the major indexes, such as the MSCI EAFE Index and the S&P 500 Index. Options and futures are traded on exchanges and so are processed through a clearing house. That matters because a clearing house eliminates virtually all of the default risk present in having a contract with a single counterparty: the exchange becomes the effective counterparty. Equity swaps, on the other hand, are generally executed with a single counterparty and so add the risk of default by that counterparty.
rationales.B: The counterparty risk profiles are not identical. Exchange clearing effectively eliminates default risk on listed options and futures because the clearing house, backed by the exchange, stands between the two sides and collects margin. An equity swap executed bilaterally with a single counterparty retains exposure to that counterparty's default.
rationales.C: The instruments are not structurally identical. Payoff profiles differ, with options nonlinear and futures and swaps linear; trading venues differ, with options and futures listed on exchanges and equity swaps generally negotiated bilaterally; and clearing arrangements differ, which is what drives the difference in counterparty default risk.

questions.stem: Derivatives leverage through notional value most likely means:

options.A: notional value can be many times the initial cash outlay.
options.B: exchange rules cap leverage at twice the cash outlay.
options.C: notional value equals the margin the buyer posts.

rationales.A: Derivatives allow for leverage through their notional value amounts: the notional value of the contracts can be many times greater than the initial cash outlay, so a small amount of capital controls a large exposure. The offsetting feature is that derivatives expire, whereas stocks can be held indefinitely. The risk of an expiring options contract is a complete loss of the relatively small premium paid to acquire the exposure. Futures and swaps can be extended by rolling the contract forward, which means selling the expiring contract and buying a longer-dated one.
rationales.B: No such ceiling exists. Exchanges set margin requirements and can impose position limits, but neither amounts to a cap on leverage at twice the cash outlay. The notional value of derivative contracts can be many times greater than the initial cash outlay, and that gap is the source of the leverage.
rationales.C: Margin is a small fraction of notional value, posted as collateral to reduce the credit risk borne by the exchange. If margin equalled notional value there would be no leverage at all. The gap between the initial cash outlay and the much larger notional exposure is precisely what makes a derivative position levered.

questions.stem: Overlays are most likely:

options.A: derivative positions used to adjust an existing portfolio toward its objectives.
options.B: cash-market trades used to permanently restructure the portfolio.
options.C: a fund's primary long-term investment strategy.

rationales.A: Derivatives are typically used to adjust a pre-existing portfolio to move it closer to meeting its objectives, and these derivative positions are often referred to as an overlay. There are three common types. A completion overlay addresses an indexed portfolio that has diverged from its proper exposure, as when a surplus of cash built up from investor flows or dividends leaves the portfolio's beta significantly below the benchmark's. A rebalancing overlay addresses a portfolio's need to sell certain constituent securities and buy others; particularly in a mixed stock and bond portfolio, using equity index derivatives to rebalance toward investment policy target weights can be efficient and cost effective. A currency overlay hedges the returns of securities held in a foreign currency back to the home currency.
rationales.B: An overlay is a derivative position, not a cash-market trade, and its purpose is to adjust a pre-existing portfolio toward its objectives rather than to restructure it permanently. Completion, rebalancing, and currency overlays all sit on top of an existing exposure and are unwound or rolled as the need changes; permanent, strategic restructuring is where cash instruments are the better tool.
rationales.C: It is uncommon for index-based portfolio managers to use derivatives over the long term to synthetically mimic the return from the underlying securities. Overlays are adjustment tools layered onto a pre-existing portfolio, correcting diverged exposure, rebalancing toward policy weights, or hedging foreign currency exposure, rather than the portfolio's primary strategy.

questions.stem: Equity index derivative advantages over cash-based portfolio construction most likely include:

options.A: unlimited position size, free of exchange-imposed limits.
options.B: single-transaction adjustment of exposure to the entire index.
options.C: complete elimination of tracking error versus the index.

rationales.A: Position size is not unlimited. Futures markets can impose position limits that constrain the scale on which derivatives can be used, margin must be posted as collateral, and derivatives usage is sometimes restricted by regulatory bodies or investment policy statement stipulations. The advantage derivatives offer is efficient, liquid, single-transaction adjustment of exposure, not unbounded size.
rationales.B: Equity index derivatives offer several advantages over cash-based portfolio construction approaches. A portfolio manager can increase or decrease exposure to the entire index portfolio in a single transaction. Managers who want to make tactical adjustments to portfolio exposure often find derivatives to be a more efficient tool than cash-market transactions for achieving their goals. Many derivatives contracts are highly liquid, sometimes more so than the underlying cash assets, and in that case portfolio exposures can be tactically adjusted quickly and at low cost.
rationales.C: Tracking error is not eliminated. A derivatives overlay introduces its own sources of divergence from the index, including basis risk between the futures price and the spot index, the cost and timing of rolling expiring contracts, and the return earned on the cash collateral held against the position. What derivatives deliver is quick, low-cost adjustment of exposure, not perfect replication.

questions.stem: For strategic, long-term changes to a portfolio's index exposure, it is most likely that:

options.A: derivatives are superior to cash instruments in every case.
options.B: cash instruments are generally preferred to derivatives.
options.C: cash instruments are never used, derivatives dominating on cost.

rationales.A: Derivatives are not superior in every case. They have finite expirations, so maintaining a long-horizon position requires repeatedly rolling contracts, which is costly. Futures markets can impose position limits that constrain the scale of use. Derivatives usage is sometimes restricted by regulatory bodies or investment policy statement stipulations. And depending on the index being tracked, a suitable exchange-traded futures contract may not be available at all. Derivatives are the better tool for tactical, temporary adjustments; cash instruments suit strategic, long-horizon positions.
rationales.B: For the longer term, strategic changes to portfolios are usually best made using cash instruments, which have indefinite expirations and do not necessitate rolling over expiring positions. Futures markets can impose position limits on such instruments that constrain the scale of use. Derivatives usage is also sometimes restricted by regulatory bodies or investment policy statement stipulations, so cash could be the preferred approach on those grounds alone. Finally, depending on the index that is being tracked, a suitable exchange-traded futures contract may not be available.
rationales.C: Cash instruments are in fact the standard vehicle for long-term index exposure, precisely because they have indefinite expirations and need no rolling of expiring positions. Cost is not the deciding consideration, and the costs run the other way once rolling is accounted for. Derivatives are also subject to position limits and to regulatory or investment policy statement restrictions, and a suitable exchange-traded contract may not exist for the index being tracked.

questions.stem: Equity index futures most likely are:

options.A: settled by physical delivery of the index constituents.
options.B: settled by delivery of an exchange-traded fund tracking the index.
options.C: settled in cash rather than in the underlying shares.

rationales.A: Unlike many commodity futures contracts, equity index futures involve no physical delivery of the underlying. Delivering several hundred constituent securities in index weights at every expiration would be impractical, so the counterparties exchange cash equal to the change in contract value instead.
rationales.B: Index futures are cash-settled, so no securities change hands at settlement, whether constituent shares or shares of a fund tracking the index. The exchange-traded fund is a separate vehicle for obtaining index exposure, not the deliverable against a futures contract.
rationales.C: Alongside options, which have nonlinear payoffs, the two primary types of equity index derivatives contracts are futures and swaps. Equity index futures provide exposure to a specific index, and unlike many commodity futures contracts they are cash-settled, which means the counterparties exchange cash rather than the underlying shares. The buyer of an equity index futures contract obtains the right to buy the underlying, in this case an index, on the expiration date of the contract at the futures price prevailing at the time the derivative was purchased. For exchange-traded futures, the buyer is required to post margin as collateral in the account to decrease the credit risk to the exchange, which is the effective counterparty.

questions.stem: The contract multiplier for S&P 500 Index futures traded on the Chicago Mercantile Exchange is closest to:

rationales.A: A multiplier of 1 would make the contract value equal to the index level itself, which is not how the contract is specified. For S&P 500 Index futures as traded on the Chicago Mercantile Exchange, every one-dollar change in the futures price produces a 250-dollar change in contract value.
rationales.B: For S&P 500 Index futures contracts as traded on the Chicago Mercantile Exchange, every USD change in the futures price produces a USD 250 change in the contract value, which is the multiplier of 250. For example, if the September S&P 500 futures contract settled at a price of 2,159.30 after settling at 2,157 the day before, the change in contract value would be 250 × (USD 2,159.30 − USD 2,157) = USD 575. Other index futures carry their own multipliers: Dow Jones mini USD 5, S&P 500 mini USD 50, NASDAQ 100 mini USD 20, Euro STOXX 50 EUR 10, FTSE 100 GBP 10, DAX 30 EUR 25, Nikkei 225 JPY 1,000, and KOSPI 200 KRW 500,000.
rationales.C: USD 5 is the multiplier on the Dow Jones mini contract, not on the full-size S&P 500 Index futures contract. The full-size S&P 500 contract carries a multiplier of 250, so a one-dollar move in the futures price changes contract value by USD 250.

questions.stem: The role of a futures commission merchant (FCM) is most likely that of:

options.A: An exchange employee setting margin levels.
options.B: A self-clearing investor acting without an intermediary.
options.C: A clearing house member trading on the investor's behalf.

rationales.A: Initial and maintenance margin levels are set by the clearing house, not by the FCM and not by an employee of the exchange. The FCM is a clearing house member assigned to trade on behalf of the investor: it posts the initial margin required to open the position, settles on a daily basis to comply with the maintenance margin required by the clearing house, and helps close the position upon expiration. Its function is execution and clearing for the client, not the setting of margin requirements.
rationales.B: The FCM is an essential intermediary, not an arrangement the investor can dispense with by clearing its own trades. Futures positions must be initiated with a futures commission merchant, a clearing house member assigned to trade on behalf of the investor. The investor's own effort does not disappear either: having a futures account requires management of daily cash flows, sometimes committing additional money and sometimes drawing it down.
rationales.C: The FCM is a clearing house member assigned to trade on behalf of the investor for futures positions. It posts the initial margin required to open the position, then settles on a daily basis to comply with the maintenance margin required by the clearing house, and it also helps close the position upon expiration. Futures accounts are not free of effort on the client's part: holding one requires the management of daily cash flows, sometimes committing additional money to the account and sometimes drawing it down.

questions.stem: Relative to short-selling stocks, opening a short equity index futures position is most likely:

options.A: Free of the short-sale constraints many institutions face.
options.B: Subject to the same constraints as stock short sales.
options.C: Prohibited for most institutional investors.

rationales.A: Many institutional investors face short-sale constraints on stock positions, but many of those same investors do not face constraints on opening a futures position with a sale of the contracts. The futures market therefore provides an easy shorting mechanism relative to cash equities. Among the other benefits of futures is the high degree of liquidity in the market, as evidenced by low bid-ask spreads, and both commission and execution costs tend to be low relative to the exposure achieved. That low cost of transacting makes it easy for portfolio managers to use futures contracts to modify the equity risk exposure of their portfolios.
rationales.B: The constraints are not the same. Many institutional investors who face short-sale constraints on stock positions do not face constraints on opening a futures position with a sale of the contracts, which is precisely why futures are used to take short equity exposure efficiently.
rationales.C: Selling index futures is widely permitted rather than prohibited. With a high degree of liquidity, low bid-ask spreads, and low commission and execution costs relative to the exposure achieved, futures provide an easy shorting mechanism relative to cash equities.

questions.stem: Equity index swaps are most likely:

options.A: Exchange-traded.
options.B: Centrally cleared, removing counterparty risk.
options.C: Over-the-counter, carrying counterparty default risk.

rationales.A: Equity swaps are over-the-counter instruments, not exchange-traded ones. Futures are the exchange-traded alternative; swaps are negotiated bilaterally, which is what introduces counterparty default risk.
rationales.B: Unlike exchange-traded futures, which are backed by a clearing house, equity swaps are generally executed with a single counterparty and so add the risk of default by that counterparty. No central clearing house stands between the two sides to remove that risk.
rationales.C: Equity index swaps are over-the-counter contracts, generally executed with a single counterparty, which adds the risk of default by that counterparty. This distinguishes them from futures, which are exchange-traded and cleared. Because swaps are over-the-counter, counterparty selection matters. They are sometimes used strategically to synthetically mimic an index return, may serve for tactical adjustments or currency hedging as overlays, and can be extended by rolling into a new agreement.

questions.stem: The choice among pooled investments, derivatives, or SMAs for index exposure most likely depends on:

options.A: The investor's tax status alone.
options.B: No identifiable factors.
options.C: Investor size and the cost-effectiveness of self-management.

rationales.A: Taxes matter, but they sit among several considerations rather than being the single determinant. Investor size and the cost-effectiveness of self-managed replication lead the list, alongside cost and flexibility trade-offs, regulatory and investment policy statement constraints, index availability, and whether the exposure is strategic or tactical.
rationales.B: The choice is far from arbitrary. Size, costs, horizon, in-house expertise, and the intended use case systematically drive whether an investor uses a pooled fund, a derivative, or a separate account.
rationales.C: Investor size is the leading consideration: large investors find it more cost effective to build their own portfolios through replication, stratified sampling, and optimization, while smaller investors prefer pooled vehicles, and other investors find exchange-traded funds a relatively low-cost method of tracking major indexes. Further trade-offs follow: strategic exposure favors cash instruments while tactical exposure makes derivatives efficient; regulatory constraints may limit derivatives use; an exchange-traded futures contract must exist on the index being tracked; and individual investors often face access difficulties with derivatives.

questions.stem: Basis risk on an equity index futures position is most likely best described as:

options.A: Default risk on the clearing house.
options.B: A risk removed by daily settlement.
options.C: The risk that futures and spot prices diverge.

rationales.A: Clearing house default is counterparty or credit risk, and the clearing house structure exists to mitigate it. Basis risk is a separate and distinct exposure: the risk that futures and spot prices do not move in concert.
rationales.B: Daily marking to market manages credit exposure between the parties by settling gains and losses as they accrue. It does nothing to prevent futures and spot prices from diverging, so basis risk remains after every daily settlement.
rationales.C: Basis risk is the risk that futures and spot prices do not move in concert. Index fund managers use equity index futures because the instruments are expected to move in line with the underlying index; to the extent that the futures and spot prices do not move together, the manager may see performance divergence from the intended index-tracking outcome. Even the excellent match between futures and spot prices is not a perfect one, and the residual mismatch creates tracking error.

drills.los_text: compare the full replication, stratified sampling, and optimization approaches for the construction of index-based equity portfolios

questions.stem: An index-based portfolio built by full replication most likely holds:

options.A: All constituents at equal weights.
options.B: All constituents at index weights.
options.C: A small sample of constituents.

rationales.A: Full replication holds every constituent in the same proportion as the index, not at equal weights. Equal weighting would create deliberate size tilts against the index and would itself become a source of tracking error.
rationales.B: Full replication holds all the constituent securities of the index in the same proportion as the index, which provides the tightest tracking. It requires a large-scale portfolio and high-quality information about the constituent characteristics. The portfolio manager must then maintain the portfolio in line with index changes, making those changes in a timely manner to preserve performance tracking, and a perfectly replicated index portfolio must trade at the market-on-close price where available in order to match the price used by the index provider in calculating index performance.
rationales.C: Holding a limited number of names is sampling, not replication. Stratified sampling deliberately accepts some tracking error in exchange for lower trading and maintenance costs; full replication accepts the cost in order to hold the complete index.

questions.stem: Stratified sampling most likely involves:

options.A: Grouping constituents into mutually exclusive, exhaustive strata.
options.B: Holding every index constituent at equal weights.
options.C: Drawing constituents at random from the full index.

rationales.A: To stratify is to arrange a population into distinct strata, or subgroupings. Arranged correctly, the various strata are mutually exclusive and also exhaustive, a complete set, and they should closely match the characteristics and performance of the index. Common stratification approaches include industry membership and equity style characteristics: investors tracking the S&P 500 commonly assign each stock to one of the eleven sectors designated by the Global Industry Classification Standard. For multinational indexes, stratification is often done first on the basis of country affiliation and then by industry within each country.
rationales.B: Holding every index constituent is full replication rather than sampling, and replication matches index proportions rather than equal weights. Stratified sampling holds a representative subset of names within each stratum.
rationales.C: The sampling is not done randomly. Names are selected within mutually exclusive and exhaustive strata that are matched to the characteristics and performance of the index, and holdings tend to be weighted proportionately to each stratum's weight in the index. Simple random draws would not preserve those characteristics.

questions.stem: Stratified sampling is most likely used when:

options.A: The index has thousands of constituents or assets under management are small.
options.B: Trading resources are unlimited and zero tracking error is required.
options.C: The index has few, highly liquid constituents.

rationales.A: In equity indexing, stratified sampling is most frequently used when the portfolio manager wants to track indexes that have many constituents or when dealing with a relatively low level of assets under management. Indexes with many constituents are usually multi-country or multi-cap indexes, such as the S&P Global Broad Market Index, which consists of more than 11,000 constituents. Most investors are reluctant to trade and maintain 11,000 securities when a significantly smaller number of constituents would achieve most portfolios' tracking objectives. Whatever stratification approach is used, index-based managers tend to weight portfolio holdings proportionately to each stratum's weight in the index.
rationales.B: Unlimited trading resources and a demand for the tightest possible tracking point toward full replication. Stratified sampling exists to economize on trading and maintenance costs, and it accepts a small amount of tracking error in exchange.
rationales.C: An index with a small number of highly liquid names invites full replication, since all of its constituents can be bought and maintained cheaply. Sampling earns its keep on broad indexes with thousands of names, or in illiquid segments, where holding everything is impractical.

questions.stem: Optimization for an index-based portfolio most likely involves:

options.A: Applying stratified sampling under another name.
options.B: Minimizing tracking error without constraints.
options.C: Minimizing tracking error subject to constraints.

rationales.A: Optimization is a distinct technique. It solves a formal objective function, such as minimizing tracking error, subject to stated constraints, rather than arranging the index into strata whose characteristics the portfolio is built to match.
rationales.B: Constraints are integral to the formulation, not optional. The number of holdings, market capitalization floors, style characteristics, round lots, and limits that keep rebalancing costs low all enter the problem; an unconstrained minimization is not how an indexed portfolio is optimized.
rationales.C: Optimization typically involves maximizing a desirable characteristic or minimizing an undesirable characteristic, subject to one or more constraints. For an indexed portfolio, that could mean minimizing index tracking error subject to the constraint that the portfolio holds 50 constituent securities or fewer, with the desired output being the identification of those 50 securities and the weights that result in the lowest possible tracking error. The number of holdings is not the only possible constraint: others commonly include limiting membership to stocks above a specified market capitalization, style characteristics that mimic those of the benchmark, restricting trades to round lots, and using only stocks that will keep rebalancing costs low.

questions.stem: An optimization that minimizes index tracking error is most likely to:

options.A: Leave portfolio volatility unrelated to tracking error.
options.B: Produce a portfolio riskier than the benchmark.
options.C: Produce a mean-variance efficient portfolio.

rationales.A: The two are linked rather than unrelated. The research on this point analyzes precisely how a tracking error constraint distorts the volatility and return trade-off of the resulting portfolio, which is why a separate constraint on total portfolio volatility is needed.
rationales.B: Running an optimization to minimize tracking error can lead to portfolios that are mean-variance inefficient versus the benchmark: the optimized portfolio may exhibit higher risk than the benchmark it is being optimized against, as Roll (1992) and Jorion (2003) demonstrate. A useful way to address this problem is to add a constraint on total portfolio volatility, so the manager of an optimized index-based fund would aim to make the fund's total volatility equal to that of the benchmark.
rationales.C: The finding runs the other way. Tracking-error-minimizing portfolios can be mean-variance inefficient versus the benchmark and may carry higher total risk than it, which is why a constraint equating total portfolio volatility to benchmark volatility is added.

questions.stem: Compared with stratified sampling, an advantage of optimization is most likely:

options.A: lower tracking error.
options.B: no periodic re-estimation of inputs.
options.C: lower cost and less technical sophistication.

rationales.A: Optimization produces a lower amount of tracking error than stratified sampling, because the optimization process accounts explicitly for the covariances among the portfolio constituents. Two securities from different industry sectors may both be included in a portfolio under stratified sampling, but if their returns move strongly together, one of them will likely be excluded from an optimized portfolio.
rationales.B: Optimization relies on estimated returns, variances, and covariances among the constituents, and those relationships tend to vary over time, so the inputs must be re-estimated and the optimization re-run periodically, with costly portfolio adjustments each time.
rationales.C: Optimization is more complex and more data-intensive than stratified sampling and requires an analyst with a high level of technical sophistication, including familiarity with computerized optimization software and a good understanding of its output. Its advantages are lower tracking error and the explicit treatment of covariances, not lower cost or simplicity.

questions.stem: An optimization approach to index portfolio construction is most likely:

options.A: constrained by its use of past market data.
options.B: free of disadvantages relative to sampling.
options.C: based on forward-looking market forecasts.

rationales.A: The constituents and weights of an optimized portfolio are usually determined on the basis of past market data; however, returns, variances, and correlations between securities tend to vary over time. The output from an optimization program may therefore apply only to the period from which the data are drawn and not to a future period, and even if current results do apply to the future, they might not be applicable for long. Optimization would then need to be run frequently and adjustments made to the portfolio, which can be costly. It also requires an analyst with a high level of technical sophistication, including familiarity with computerized optimization software or algorithms and a good understanding of the output.
rationales.B: Optimization's estimates of returns, variances, and correlations are backward-looking, and it requires costly re-runs and portfolio adjustments as those relationships shift, so it carries real disadvantages relative to replication and sampling.
rationales.C: The inputs are past data — returns, variances, and correlations — and these vary over time, so the output may apply only to the period from which the data were drawn rather than to a future period.

questions.stem: A blended approach to constructing an indexed portfolio is most likely to:

options.A: replicate the liquid issues and sample the less-liquid issues.
options.B: be prohibited, as one method must cover the entire index.
options.C: alternate replication and sampling by calendar quarter.

rationales.A: For indexes that have few constituent securities, full replication is typically advisable; when the reverse is true, sampling or optimization are likely to be the preferred methods. But indexes such as the Russell 3000, the S&P 1500, and the Wilshire 5000 span the capitalization spectrum from large to small. For these indexes the 1,000 or so largest constituents are quite liquid, which means brokerage fees, bid-ask spreads, and trading costs are low, so full replication is a sensible and desirable approach for the largest-cap portion of the portfolio. For constituents with smaller market capitalizations or less liquidity, a stratified sampling or optimization approach can be useful. An indexed portfolio can therefore be managed using a blended approach: full replication for the more-liquid issues and one of the other methods for the less-liquid issues.
rationales.B: Combining construction methods by liquidity segment is standard practice for indexes that span capitalization tiers, and nothing requires a single method to be applied across the whole index.
rationales.C: The blend is cross-sectional rather than time-varying: full replication is applied to the liquid names and stratified sampling or optimization to the illiquid ones, within the same portfolio and at the same time.

questions.stem: In practice, index-based portfolio managers' use of mean-variance optimization is most likely:

options.A: undocumented in the practitioner literature.
options.B: conducted using all index constituents.
options.C: completed in a single stage.

rationales.A: The practice is documented in practitioner research, which describes managers optimizing across the full list of index constituents and then pruning the smallest weights.
rationales.B: In practice, index-based portfolio managers often conduct a mean-variance optimization using all the index constituents, the output from which shows highly diverse weightings for the stocks. Given that investing in the lowest-weight stocks may involve marginal transaction costs that exceed the marginal diversification benefits, in a second, post-optimization stage the managers may then delete the lowest-weighted stocks.
rationales.C: The practice has two stages: an optimization across all index constituents, followed by a post-optimization step in which the lowest-weighted stocks are deleted because their marginal transaction costs exceed their marginal diversification benefits.

questions.stem: A client with $750,000 to invest wants a portfolio that tracks the S&P 500 Value Index, which holds more than 300 constituents. The manager's recommendation is most likely to:

options.A: hold all 300-plus constituents.
options.B: cap holdings at 200, selected by largest market capitalization.
options.C: cap holdings at 200, selected by lowest price volatility.

rationales.A: Spreading $750,000 across more than 300 constituents forces very small average lot sizes and high commission costs, so the manager samples the index and reweights the sample rather than replicating it in full.
rationales.B: The manager recommends that the client set a maximum number of constituents, for example 200, to limit the average lot size and to reduce commission costs. The manager then identifies the constituents to hold on the basis of their market capitalization, selecting the 200 securities with the largest market capitalizations. To more closely match the performance of the index, the manager compares the sector weightings of the sampled portfolio with the sector weightings of the index and reweights the sampled portfolio accordingly.
rationales.C: The 200 holdings are identified by largest market capitalization, not by lowest price volatility; the sampled portfolio's sector weights are then compared with the index's and reweighted to match.

questions.stem: Full replication is most likely preferred for an index that has:

options.A: few constituent securities.
options.B: many illiquid constituents.
options.C: thousands of small-cap, illiquid constituents.

rationales.A: For indexes that have few constituent securities, full replication is typically advisable; when the reverse is true, sampling or optimization are likely to be the preferred methods. Full replication requires a large-scale portfolio and high-quality information about the constituents, so it works best when the constituents are few and liquid, where replication is straightforward and cost-effective. The large-cap portions of broad indexes support full replication for the same reason: high liquidity keeps brokerage fees, spreads, and trading costs low.
rationales.B: Illiquid constituents are expensive to buy in index weight and expensive to maintain, which pushes the manager toward sampling or optimization; full replication is preferred when the constituents are few and liquid.
rationales.C: When an index has many constituents or hard-to-find, illiquid securities, sampling or optimization is the preferred method, because replicating thousands of small, illiquid positions carries prohibitive trading costs. Full replication is advisable when the constituents are few and liquid.

questions.stem: Model-portfolio matching using an order management system (OMS) most likely involves:

options.A: delivery of orders by email.
options.B: post-trade compliance checks only.
options.C: spreadsheet and database modeling of weight differences.

rationales.A: The OMS is used to deliver the buy and sell orders for execution using the FIX or SWIFT protocol, not by email.
rationales.B: The OMS is programmed to provide the investor with pre-trade compliance, checking for client-specific restrictions, front-running issues, and other compliance rules before orders are sent for execution, so compliance is not limited to post-trade review.
rationales.C: This type of modeling, which compares current weights with model weights to derive the variance and the number of shares to trade, can easily and cheaply be conducted using spreadsheet and database programs such as Excel and Access. The modeling is only part of the portfolio management process: the OMS should also be programmed to provide pre-trade compliance, checking for client-specific restrictions, front-running issues, and other compliance rules, and it is used to deliver the buy and sell orders for execution using the FIX or SWIFT protocol. After the initial creation of the indexed portfolio, the manager must maintain the portfolio according to any changes in the index; those changes are announced publicly by the index provider, and index fund managers use the details to update their models in the OMS and to determine the number of shares to buy or sell.

questions.stem: The choice among full replication, stratified sampling, and optimization most likely depends on:

options.A: the fund's expense ratio target alone.
options.B: manager preference, as the approaches involve no trade-offs.
options.C: constituent count, liquidity, assets under management, and cost against tracking error.

rationales.A: The number of index constituents, their liquidity, the size of assets under management, the manager's technical sophistication, and the cost versus tracking-error trade-off all bear on the choice; an expense ratio target is an outcome of those decisions rather than the single factor driving them.
rationales.B: Each approach trades tracking precision against trading cost and operational complexity differently, so the decision rests on real trade-offs rather than style.
rationales.C: The choice depends on the number of index constituents, the liquidity of those constituents, the size of assets under management, the technical sophistication of the manager, the cost versus tracking-error trade-off, and whether the portfolio must accommodate specific covariance structures. Many-constituent indexes call for sampling or optimization to reduce trading costs; illiquid constituents make full replication expensive; small assets under management make replication impractical because of minimum lot sizes; and optimization requires technical sophistication. Blended approaches are also common for broad indexes, combining full replication for the liquid large caps with sampling or optimization for the smaller or less liquid names.

drills.los_text: discuss potential causes of tracking error and methods to control tracking error for index-based equity portfolios

questions.stem: Tracking error is most likely defined as:

options.A: the standard deviation of portfolio return minus benchmark return.
options.B: the average portfolio return.
options.C: the portfolio's excess return.

rationales.A: Tracking error indicates how closely the portfolio behaves like its benchmark and measures a manager's ability to replicate the benchmark return. It is calculated as the standard deviation of the difference between the portfolio return and its benchmark index return: TE = the square root of Variance(Rp - Rb). Being a standard deviation, tracking error is always presented as a non-negative number.
rationales.B: Tracking error is a standard deviation, not an average: it measures the dispersion of the return difference between portfolio and benchmark, and as a standard deviation it is always non-negative.
rationales.C: Excess return is a distinct measure, equal to Rp - Rb, and it can be positive or negative. Tracking error is the standard deviation of that difference, so the two terms should not be used interchangeably.

questions.stem: Excess return is most likely:

options.A: always positive.
options.B: the difference between portfolio and benchmark returns.
options.C: the same as tracking error.

rationales.A: Excess returns can be positive or negative, and they tell the investor how the manager performed relative to the benchmark. Index fund managers endeavor to have non-negative excess returns, but nothing in the measure makes it positive by construction.
rationales.B: Excess return measures the difference between the portfolio returns and the benchmark returns: Excess returnp = Rp - Rb. It can be positive or negative and tells the investor how the manager performed relative to the benchmark, which is why index fund managers endeavor to have non-negative excess returns.
rationales.C: Tracking error and excess return are distinct measures and the terms should not be used interchangeably. Tracking error measures the manager's ability to closely track the benchmark over time. In principle, a manager whose return is identical to that of the index could have arrived at that point by lagging and subsequently leading the index, producing a net difference of zero; but being a standard deviation, tracking error cannot be zero in such a case.

questions.stem: Compared with an index that has few constituents, an index with a large number of constituents most likely produces tracking error that is:

options.A: the same.
options.B: lower.
options.C: higher.

rationales.A: Constituent count is a systematic driver of tracking difficulty, so tracking error is not independent of it. The number of securities a fund holds relative to its benchmark is one of the primary sources of tracking error: a manager who cannot hold every name must sample, and a sampled portfolio's returns deviate from the index's.
rationales.B: The relationship runs in the opposite direction.
