A large constituent count, typically with an illiquid tail of small names, makes faithful replication harder and raises tracking error; an index with few, liquid constituents is easier to replicate in full, so it produces less deviation, not more.
rationales.C: An index that contains a large number of constituents tends to create higher tracking error than one with fewer constituents, because a large number of constituents may prevent the manager from fully replicating the index. The manager is then forced to sample, holding a subset of names chosen to approximate the index's exposures, and sampled portfolios typically report greater tracking error than those that are fully replicated. Illiquid or very small constituents at the bottom of a broad index compound the problem, since the cost of buying them at index weights can outweigh the tracking benefit.

questions.stem: A primary cause of tracking error in an indexed equity fund most likely is:

options.A: benchmark index turnover, which does not affect the fund.
options.B: securities-lending income, which always raises tracking error.
options.C: fees charged, which always reduce excess return.

rationales.A: Changes in the benchmark's constituents affect the fund as well: the manager must trade to match them, and that trading is itself a source of deviation. The primary causes of tracking error are the fees charged, the number of securities held versus the benchmark, intra-day trading prices versus closing prices, commission costs, and cash holdings.
rationales.B: Securities-lending income offsets management costs and can reduce negative excess return rather than add to deviation, so it is not among the primary causes of tracking error.
rationales.C: Tracking error in an indexed equity fund arises for several reasons: (1) the fees charged, which are always negative and drive down excess return, so higher fees contribute to lower excess returns and higher tracking error; (2) the number of securities held by the portfolio versus the benchmark index, since sampled portfolios typically report greater tracking error than those that are fully replicated; (3) intra-day trading of the constituent stocks, because the price levels used to report index returns are struck at the close of the trading day, so any security bought or sold at a price different from the index's contributes to tracking error; (4) the trading commissions paid to brokers, which make excess returns more negative and also affect tracking error; and (5) cash holdings, because equity indexes do not have a cash allocation, so any cash balance creates tracking error.

questions.stem: Cash drag most likely refers to:

options.A: tracking error caused by temporarily uninvested cash.
options.B: a return enhancement from holding riskless cash.
options.C: the excess return earned on an index fund's cash reserves.

rationales.A: Equity indexes do not have a cash allocation, so any cash balance creates tracking error for the index fund manager. Cash can be accumulated in the portfolio from a variety of sources, such as dividends received, sale proceeds, investor contributions, and other income. Cash flows from investors and from the constituent companies may not be invested immediately, and investing them often entails a commission cost, so both affect tracking error. The tracking error caused by temporarily uninvested cash is known as cash drag, and its effect on portfolio value is negative when the market is rising and positive when it is falling.
rationales.B: Uninvested cash lags the index in a rising market, which is the classic drag; and direction aside, the deviation itself is the problem, because cash drag names a source of tracking error rather than a reliable addition to return. That cash is riskless is precisely why it fails to keep up with an equity benchmark.
rationales.C: The term names the tracking error caused by uninvested cash, not a return bonus. Any yield earned on a cash balance is far smaller than the equity return the index assumes on that weight, so the cash position normally subtracts from relative performance in rising markets and adds to it in falling ones.

questions.stem: For an index fund manager, transacting at the market-on-close price most likely:

options.A: has no effect on tracking error.
options.B: raises tracking error.
options.C: lowers tracking error.

rationales.A: Index returns are struck at closing prices, so the execution price relative to the close is exactly what determines this component of deviation. Matching the closing print directly reduces the gap between fund and index returns.
rationales.B: Whatever volatility the closing auction carries, transacting at the same prices the index uses aligns fund and index returns. It is trading away from the close, at intra-day prices, that leaves a deviation.
rationales.C: The intra-day trading of the constituent stocks of an indexed portfolio is an important source of tracking error, and its effect can be positive or negative for the portfolio's returns compared with its benchmark index. The price levels used to report index returns are struck at the close of the trading day, so any securities bought or sold at a price different from that of the index will contribute to portfolio tracking error. Index fund managers can minimize this type of tracking error by transacting at the market-on-close price or as near to the closing time as feasible.

questions.stem: Equitizing an index portfolio's cash with futures or ETFs most likely:

options.A: neutralizes cash drag.
options.B: lowers commission costs.
options.C: raises tracking error.

rationales.A: Equitization addresses cash drag, the tracking error created by cash that is temporarily uninvested. Hill and Cheong (1996) discuss how to equitize a portfolio that would otherwise suffer from cash drag; one method is to use futures contracts, and ETFs have been used widely for the same purpose. Some portfolio managers establish a futures commission merchant relationship to offset their cash positions with a futures contract that represents the replicated index, and a manager doing this will also calculate the accrued dividends in order to hedge dividend drag, which is the cash drag attributable to accrued cash dividends paid to shareholders.
rationales.B: Equitization addresses cash drag, the tracking error created by uninvested cash, by taking index exposure through futures or ETFs. It does not reduce the commissions paid on trades in the underlying constituents; the derivative overlay carries a transaction cost of its own.
rationales.C: Equitization solves cash drag rather than adding to deviation. Giving the uninvested cash the index's market exposure brings the portfolio's return closer to the benchmark's, which lowers tracking error instead of raising it.

questions.stem: Compared with active managers whose counterparties suspect them of possessing an information advantage, trading costs for index-based portfolio managers are most likely:

options.A: lower.
options.B: the same.
options.C: higher.

rationales.A: Commission costs are a secondary component of trading costs that contributes to tracking error: they make excess returns more negative and also affect tracking error. According to Perold and Salomon (1991), the trading cost for index-based portfolio managers is likely to be lower than the trading cost for active managers who are suspected by their counterparties of possessing an information advantage. An index manager's order flow is predictable and uninformed, so liquidity providers require less compensation for taking the other side of it.
rationales.B: A difference exists rather than none. Because an index manager's flow is uninformed, counterparties price it more cheaply than flow they suspect of carrying information, so the two groups do not face the same trading cost.
rationales.C: The finding runs the other way. Counterparties who fear they are trading against information widen their terms for active managers, so it is active trading cost, not index trading cost, that is the higher of the two.

questions.stem: To control tracking error, an index-based portfolio manager most likely:

options.A: targets a portfolio beta slightly above 1.0.
options.B: minimizes the cash held in the portfolio.
options.C: holds a large cash position.

rationales.A: Managers aim to maintain a beta of 1.0 relative to the benchmark index while keeping other risk factor exposures similar to those of the index. Deliberately running beta above 1.0 is an active bet that adds tracking error rather than controlling it, and it cannot be relied on to offset fee drag, since it loses money relative to the index whenever the market falls.
rationales.B: The process of controlling tracking error involves trade-offs between the benefits and the costs of maintaining complete faithfulness to the benchmark index. An unconstrained manager would keep the number of constituent securities and their weights as closely aligned to the benchmark index as possible, yet trading costs and other fees still cause actual performance to deviate from index performance: managers trade to accommodate inflows and outflows of investor cash, to reinvest dividends, and to reflect changes in the constituents of the underlying index. Most index-based portfolio managers therefore attempt to minimize cash held, because a cash position generally creates undesirable tracking error. To keep tracking error low they invest cash flows received at the same valuations used by the benchmark index provider, net investor inflows against redemptions, and use equitization tools where immediate investment is not feasible; because investing at the provider's valuations is not always possible, they also aim to maintain a beta of 1.0 relative to the benchmark index while keeping other risk factor exposures similar to those of the index.
rationales.C: The target is a beta of 1.0 relative to the benchmark index, and a large cash balance pulls the portfolio's beta below that. Equity indexes have no cash allocation, so holding much cash creates precisely the undesirable tracking error the manager is trying to suppress.

questions.stem: An index fund's measured tracking error most likely:

options.A: is higher when computed from monthly data than from daily data.
options.B: is unchanged across data frequencies once annualized.
options.C: is different at a daily frequency than at a lower frequency.

rationales.A: There is no fixed ordering between frequencies. The point is that the measured value differs with the data frequency, and for an index fund the degree of tracking error also fluctuates over time, so neither monthly nor daily measurement is reliably the larger of the two.
rationales.B: Annualization does not remove the frequency effect. The standard deviation of return differences depends on the interval over which those differences are measured, so the tracking error value will differ depending on whether the data frequency is daily or less frequent, even after the figure has been scaled to an annual basis.
rationales.C: For an index fund, the degree of tracking error fluctuates over time, and the value will differ depending on whether the data frequency is daily or less frequent. Daily, monthly, and annual measurement produce different tracking error values because return volatility scales with the length of the measurement period and because short-interval deviations in opposite directions can offset one another when returns are measured over longer intervals.

questions.stem: Over the same period, a group of Australian index funds reported annualized tracking error of less than one-tenth the level reported by a group of Korean index funds tracking their own local index. The most likely explanation is that:

options.A: the Australian funds hold more constituents and charge lower fees.
options.B: the Korean funds hold more constituents than their index.
options.C: the two groups hold identical portfolios.

rationales.A: The Australian funds hold far more of their index's constituents than the Korean funds do, and they charge lower explicit fees. Comparing the number of stocks in each fund with the number of index constituents shows that most funds are attempting to replicate; two of them hold only 80% to 90% of the stocks in the index, which indicates that they are more likely to be using sampling, and no fund contains the same number of stocks as its index has constituents, so it is not surprising that none tracked its index perfectly. On an annualized basis, tracking error for the Australian funds is less than one-tenth the level of the Korean funds, and the negative excess returns of two of the Australian funds are relatively close to each other and possibly attributable to their management fees of 18-20 basis points.
rationales.B: Only one fund in the Korean group actually holds more stocks than its index contains, which can happen if buffering is used; the other two hold 80% to 90% of the index constituents, that is, they sample. The driver of the gap is the other way round: the Australian funds hold close to all of their index's constituents, near full replication, with low and stable fees, while the Korean funds sample.
rationales.C: The portfolios are not identical, in composition or in approach. The Australian funds are close to full replication, while two of the Korean funds hold only 80% to 90% of their index's names, which is sampling, and one holds more names than the index because of buffering. Identical portfolios would have produced similar tracking error, which is exactly what a ten-fold difference rules out.

questions.stem: Zero tracking error for an index fund most likely is:

options.A: routinely attainable with modern trading technology.
options.B: unattainable whenever the fund's return leads and lags the index.
options.C: attainable, since no property of the measure prevents it.

rationales.A: Fees, commissions, intra-day execution at prices away from the close, and cash balances all guarantee some period-by-period deviation, so a reading of zero is not something trading technology delivers routinely, however good the execution.
rationales.B: In principle, a manager whose return is identical to that of the index could have arrived at that point by lagging and subsequently leading the index, producing a net difference of zero. But being a standard deviation, tracking error cannot be zero in cases such as the one described: any per-period deviations register in the dispersion even when the cumulative difference nets out. Only truly perfect replication, with no timing differences at all, would produce a tracking error of zero.
rationales.C: The form of the measure is exactly what prevents it. Because tracking error is the standard deviation of the differences between fund and index returns, any lead-lag variation registers in it even when the cumulative difference nets to zero.

drills.los_text: explain sources of return and risk to an index-based equity portfolio

questions.stem: The sources of return for an equity index replication portfolio most likely include:

options.A: market return only.
options.B: security-selection alpha only.
options.C: company-specific, sector, country, and currency returns.

rationales.A: A replication portfolio has multiple sources of return, not market return alone. Its returns decompose in the same way as those of any actively managed fund: company-specific returns, sector returns, country returns, and currency returns all contribute, and a manager can attribute performance across each of those dimensions.
rationales.B: An index replication portfolio does not pursue security-selection alpha; by construction it holds the index constituents rather than selecting among them. Its sources of return are company-specific returns, sector returns, country returns, and currency returns, as for any fund.
rationales.C: The sources of return for an equity index replication portfolio are the same as for any actively managed fund and include company-specific returns, sector returns, country returns, and currency returns. Beyond those traditional ways of grouping the risk and return of an indexed portfolio, managers can also group holdings according to the stated portfolio objective: a high dividend yield indexed portfolio may be grouped against the broad market benchmark by dividend yield, and a low volatility portfolio may be grouped by volatility buckets.

questions.stem: Portfolio attribution analysis for an index fund most likely:

options.A: is irrelevant for an index fund.
options.B: identifies sources of return.
options.C: isolates stock-selection alpha.

rationales.A: Attribution is not irrelevant to an index fund. Even a manager tracking a broad market index needs to understand which factors are driving the returns of the portfolio and of its underlying index, and a manager of a factor-based indexed strategy needs to understand both the sources of return of the indexed portfolio and how those returns relate to the broad market index from which the constituents were drawn.
rationales.B: Most portfolio managers rely on their portfolio attribution system to help them understand the sources of return. Index fund managers who track a broad market index need to understand what factors are driving the returns of that portfolio and its underlying index. Index fund managers of factor-based strategies should understand both the sources of return for their indexed portfolios and how those returns relate to the broad market index from which the constituents were chosen; in this way, factor-based strategies are similar to actively managed funds, in the sense that they are actively chosen.
rationales.C: An index fund does not pursue stock-selection alpha, so there is no selection alpha for attribution to isolate. Attribution is used instead to understand the factors driving the returns of the portfolio and of its underlying index.

questions.stem: For an index fund with a portfolio return of 5.62% against a benchmark return of 5.65%, the difference in return most likely indicates:

options.A: close tracking of the index.
options.B: positive excess return from sector selection.
options.C: poor tracking that warrants restructuring.

rationales.A: The portfolio, with a return of 5.62%, is closely replicating the performance of its benchmark, which returned 5.65%. A portfolio that is within three basis points of its benchmark index is undoubtedly tracking the index closely. The manager would still analyze relative sector weights to identify the sources of those three basis points of return difference, but the result confirms replication rather than calling it into question.
rationales.B: The portfolio trailed the benchmark by three basis points, which is a negative excess return, not a positive one. An index fund does not pursue sector-selection skill in any case; attribution is used to locate the sources of the small difference in return.
rationales.C: A gap of only three basis points indicates very tight tracking of the benchmark, so no corrective restructuring of the portfolio is warranted.

questions.stem: Securities lending by index fund managers most likely provides:

options.A: revenue that offsets portfolio management costs.
options.B: revenue captured entirely by the lending agent.
options.C: revenue that must be passed through to the borrower.

rationales.A: Securities lending generates additional revenue that is offset against portfolio management costs, often resulting in lower net fees to investors. As of 31 March 2021, the USD 63.9 billion iShares Russell 2000 ETF (IWM) had lent USD 5.97 billion in securities to various counterparties, an amount that was 100% collateralized with cash. An affiliated party, BlackRock Institutional Trust Company, served as the securities lending agent in exchange for 4 basis points of collateral investment fees annually. IWM's net securities lending income for the year was slightly above USD 63 million, which nearly offset the approximately USD 90.7 million in investment advisory fees charged by the portfolio managers.
rationales.B: The lending agent is paid a fee for its services, but net lending income accrues to the fund and offsets management costs. For IWM, the agent earned 4 basis points of collateral investment fees annually while the fund's net lending income of slightly above USD 63 million nearly offset the approximately USD 90.7 million of advisory fees charged to investors.
rationales.C: The flow runs in the opposite direction. The lender earns the borrowing fee, and the borrower, who takes formal legal title to the securities and receives all cash flows and voting rights, must pay cash to the lender in lieu of any cash dividends received on the loaned shares.

questions.stem: Industry estimates for 30 June 2021 place the global value of securities made available for lending by institutional investors closest to:

options.A: EUR 2.6 trillion.
options.B: EUR 28 trillion.
options.C: EUR 280 billion.

rationales.A: EUR 2.6 trillion is the value actually loaned, not the value made available for lending; the two figures are reversed here. Of the EUR 28 trillion made available by institutional investors, EUR 2.6 trillion in value was on loan.
rationales.B: The 30 June 2021 global value of securities made available for lending by institutional investors was EUR 28 trillion, of which EUR 2.6 trillion in value was actually loaned. Collective investment vehicles and pension funds accounted for 59% of the total value of securities loaned. Collateral held with European triparty agents was in line with previous historical norms, with equities and government bonds representing 45% and 44% of reported collateral, respectively.
rationales.C: This understates the market by two orders of magnitude. Securities lending is a substantial market: EUR 28 trillion of securities was made available for lending by institutional investors, and even the value actually on loan, EUR 2.6 trillion, is far above this figure.

questions.stem: Securities lending risks most likely include:

options.A: no material risk to the lender.
options.B: only the permanent loss of voting rights.
options.C: credit, market, liquidity, and operational risk.

rationales.A: Securities lending carries several material risks that can offset its benefits, so it is not risk-free for the lender. The main risks are the credit quality of the borrower and the value of the posted collateral, with liquidity risk and operational risk as additional considerations.
rationales.B: Voting rights transfer to the borrower only while the shares are on loan, and the lender may sell the loaned securities at any time under the normal course of the portfolio management mandate, with the borrowed shares due back in time for normal settlement of that sale, so the loss of voting rights is neither permanent nor the principal risk. The main risks are borrower credit risk and the market risk of the posted collateral, with liquidity and operational risk as additional considerations.
rationales.C: Securities lending carries risks that can offset the benefits. The main risks are the credit quality of the borrower (credit risk) and the value of the posted collateral (market risk), although liquidity risk and operational risk are additional considerations. Lenders are permitted to sell loaned securities at any time under the normal course of the portfolio management mandate, and the borrowed shares must be returned in time for normal settlement of that sale; there is no guarantee, however, that the borrower can deliver on a timely basis. An additional risk is collateral investment risk: lenders can invest cash held as collateral, and if a lender elects to invest that cash in long-term or risky securities, the collateral value is at risk of erosion. Sigma Finance Company illustrates this risk. Sigma was a structured investment vehicle that, during the 2008-2009 global financial crisis, was downgraded by the rating agencies and lost its ability to borrow in the short-term markets, which led to default. Investors in Sigma's credit offerings, many of them securities lenders, suffered substantial losses because of the default.

questions.stem: In the securities lending market, index mutual funds and pension funds are most likely considered:

options.A: unreliable lenders.
options.B: preferred lenders.
options.C: undesirable lenders.

rationales.A: Long-term, low-turnover holders are the least likely lenders to recall shares abruptly, which makes them reliable counterparties rather than unreliable ones. Institutional investors such as index mutual funds and pension funds are therefore sought out by borrowers, not avoided.
rationales.B: Institutional investors such as index mutual funds and pension funds are viewed as preferred lenders because they are long-term holders of shares and are unlikely to claim their shares back abruptly from borrowers. That stability of holdings is precisely what a borrower values, since the borrowed shares must be returned in time for normal settlement whenever the lender does sell.
rationales.C: The holdings of index mutual funds and pension funds are notably stable, and that stability is why borrowers prefer them as lenders. Rapid portfolio turnover would be the characteristic that makes a lender undesirable, and these investors do not have it.

questions.stem: The annualized cost of borrowing a security in the securities lending market is most likely:

options.B: a fixed 25% for every security.
options.C: zero.

rationales.A: Borrowers take formal legal title to the securities, receive all cash flows and voting rights, and pay an annualized cost of borrowing that is typically 2% to 10%. The borrowing cost depends on the borrower's credit quality and on how difficult it is to borrow the security in question; some securities are widely recognized as easy to borrow (ETB) and carry a cost at the low end of that range. Borrowers must also pay cash to lenders in lieu of any cash dividends received on the loaned shares.
rationales.B: The borrowing fee is not fixed and is not uniform across securities. It varies with the borrower's credit quality and with how difficult the security is to borrow, and it typically falls in a range of 2% to 10% annualized rather than at any single high rate.
rationales.C: Securities lending is a fee business, not a market courtesy. Borrowers take formal legal title to the securities, receive all cash flows and voting rights, and pay an annualized borrowing cost that is typically 2% to 10%, with the fee depending on their credit quality and on how hard the security is to borrow.

questions.stem: Investor activism by index-based fund managers most likely involves:

options.A: no engagement with corporate management.
options.B: voting shares and private meetings on governance and strategy issues.
options.C: attending annual meetings without voting shares.

rationales.A: Not choosing the holdings is no bar to activism. Institutional investors, and especially index fund managers, are among the largest shareholders of many companies, and the shares they vote can have a large influence on corporate elections and on the outcomes of the proxy process. Their status as large shareholders also gives them access to private meetings with corporate management.
rationales.B: Institutional investors, especially index fund managers, are among the largest shareholders of many companies, and the shares they vote can have a large influence on corporate elections and the outcomes of the proxy process. Their status as large shareholders often gives such investors access to private meetings with corporate management to discuss their concerns and preferences regarding corporate policies on board structure and composition, management compensation, operational risk management, the integrity of accounting statements, and other matters. In one survey, about two-thirds of public companies indicated that investor engagement in 2014 was higher than it had been three years earlier; the typical points of contact were investor relations specialists, the general counsel or corporate secretary, the board chair, and the CEO or CFO. Engagement now covers more topics, and the subject matter is not principally financial: governance policies, executive compensation, and social, environmental, and strategy issues are dominant.
rationales.C: Voting the shares is the core mechanism of activism, not something indexers forgo, and engagement extends well beyond annual meetings to private meetings with management. The matters addressed are dominated by governance policies, executive compensation, and social, environmental, and strategy issues.

questions.stem: The rationale for governance activism by index-based managers most likely is:

options.A: that governance is irrelevant to a portfolio tracking an index.
options.B: that governance improvements raise the returns of index constituents.
options.C: that activism earns regulatory credit.

rationales.A: Across a broadly diversified portfolio, governance quality is itself broadly diversified, and index-based investors by definition do not try to select the best-performing companies or avoid the worst. That inability to sell a poorly governed company is precisely why engagement matters: improvement is the indexer's only lever, and the resulting efficiency gains flow through to the index and to the portfolio tracking it.
rationales.B: Corporate governance improvements are aimed at improving the effectiveness of the operations, management, and board oversight of the business. If the resulting efficiency improvements are evidenced in higher returns to index-constituent stocks, the index performance rises and so does the performance of an index-tracking portfolio; a goal of activism is therefore to increase returns. Index-based investors may even have a higher duty than more-transient active managers to use their influence to improve governance, because as long as a stock has membership in the benchmark index, index-based managers can be considered permanent shareholders.
rationales.C: The rationale is return-enhancing rather than regulatory. Governance activism seeks more effective operations, management, and board oversight, and the efficiency gains that follow lift the returns of index-constituent stocks and so the performance of the index-tracking portfolio.

questions.stem: Costs of activist engagement most likely include:

options.A: costs borne entirely by the proxy voting service rather than the manager.
options.B: staff resources to engage management, regulators, and other investors.
options.C: only the cost of attending annual meetings.

rationales.A: Proxy voting services such as Institutional Shareholder Services or Broadridge Financial Services are hired and paid for by the manager; the costs do not sit with the service provider. The manager also bears the staff cost of following key issues and the potential conflicts of interest that come with challenging management.
rationales.B: Among the more significant costs of engagement are the staff resources required to become familiar with key issues and to engage management, regulators, and other investors. Researching and voting thousands of proxy ballots becomes problematic for many managers, so they frequently hire a proxy voting service, such as Institutional Shareholder Services or Broadridge Financial Services, to vote the ballots in their clients' favor. A further cost is the potential conflict of interest: a financial firm managing the retirement plan of a company whose stock is an index constituent may hesitate to challenge that company's management. Shareholder return can be enhanced by engagement, but these costs must be weighed against that benefit.
rationales.C: Attending annual meetings is a minor part of the cost. Researching and voting thousands of proxy ballots is itself costly, enough that many managers outsource it to a proxy voting service, and that research is purchased by the manager rather than supplied free by issuers. The larger cost is the staff time needed to become familiar with key issues and to engage management, regulators, and other investors.

questions.stem: Time-phased voting rights most likely involve:

options.A: extra votes per share for shares held beyond a set period.
options.B: a structure that no company has adopted.
options.C: reduced voting power for long-term shareholders.

rationales.A: Reinforcing the concept of permanence, some companies give greater voting rights to long-term shareholders. Dallas and Barry (2016) examine 12 US companies whose voting rights increase to four, five, or even ten votes per share once the holding period is greater than three, and sometimes four, years. The structure suits index-based holders, whose positions are effectively permanent, and it rewards tenure rather than turnover.
rationales.B: Documented US examples exist: Dallas and Barry (2016) identify a dozen US companies with voting rights that step up to four, five, or even ten votes per share for shares held beyond three, and sometimes four, years.
rationales.C: The structure rewards tenure rather than penalizing it. Voting power increases with the length of the holding period, rising to four, five, or even ten votes per share, while shares held for less than the threshold keep their base vote. Long-term holders gain influence; they are not diluted.
